statement: The system shall keep service available and fast when any one CDN is under pressure.
The system shall not require providers to give up more control or data than they are comfortable with.
The system shall prioritize protecting user experience and meeting demand through cooperation.
The system shall prioritize preserving each provider’s privacy and commercial boundaries after user experience and demand fulfillment.
The system shall prioritize operational simplicity after user experience, demand fulfillment, and privacy concerns.
When there is a tradeoff, the system shall favor limited, policy-driven sharing over broader access to internal information.
The system shall share only the information needed to make peering work.
The system shall include privacy controls and clear opt-in policies.
The system may be more complex to set up if necessary to preserve privacy controls and clear opt-in policies.
The system shall support CDN providers as key participants because they own the capacity, policies, and content being shared.
The system shall allow each CDN provider to act through an administrator or operations team.
The provider administrator or operations team shall be able to approve peering relationships.
The provider administrator or operations team shall be able to set sharing rules.
The provider administrator or operations team shall be able to choose what data to expose.
The provider administrator or operations team shall be able to terminate arrangements when needed.
The system shall support system operators as a role when the platform is run as a shared platform or consortium service.
System operators shall be able to manage discovery.
System operators shall be able to manage routing coordination.
System operators shall be able to manage directory services without seeing everything each provider keeps private.
Automated components on each CDN shall be able to publish availability.
Automated components on each CDN shall be able to receive assignments.
Automated components on each CDN shall be able to exchange accounting data.
Automated components on each CDN shall be able to update content replication decisions within the limits of the agreed policy.
Automated components on each CDN shall be able to update request redirection decisions within the limits of the agreed policy.
The system shall let a CDN find potential peers.
The system shall allow a CDN to establish a peering agreement.
The system shall exchange the policy information and capacity information needed to support a peering arrangement.
The system shall route or redirect traffic when one side needs help.
The system shall provide basic accounting so participants can see what was used and settle afterward.
The system shall treat discovery, negotiation, request handling, and accounting flows as mandatory core capabilities.
The system may provide richer content replication strategies.
The system may provide automated optimization of peer selection.
The system may provide more detailed analytics or forecasting.
The system shall base the peer-assistance trigger on each CDN provider's own service objectives.
The system shall consider sustained origin utilization when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall consider sustained edge utilization when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall consider request queueing when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall consider cache miss pressure when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall consider error rates when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall consider latency against agreed targets when evaluating whether a CDN needs peer assistance.
The system shall request peer assistance only when the relevant metrics remain outside bounds for a defined period, not in response to a brief spike.
The system shall not hardcode the actual threshold numbers globally.
The system shall allow threshold values to be configured per provider and per service class.
The system shall support different targets for availability and latency.
The system shall support peering infrastructure that helps independent CDNs find each other.
The system shall support exchange of traffic information and accounting information between independent CDNs.
The system shall support handling capacity changes in the peering infrastructure.
The interview scope shall remain focused on peering and cooperation rather than unrelated internal CDN operations.
The system shall support CDN operations stakeholders in keeping customer traffic flowing when the CDN's own capacity becomes tight.
The CDN capacity expansion process is currently manual.
When the CDN is short on capacity, operations staff contact known partners directly.
Operations staff negotiate terms with partners over email or phone.
Operations staff configure routing or content replication by hand in separate systems.
The current process is slow.
The current process is hard to scale.
There is no clean shared way to exchange load data or accounting data.
The system shall replace ad hoc partner-by-partner handling with a more automated and repeatable process.
The system shall support faster negotiation of sharing policies.
The system shall support controlled content replication.
The system shall support traffic redirection that can react to demand with minimal manual intervention.
The system shall support the exchange of usage records.
The system shall support expanding a peering relationship.
The system shall support pausing a peering relationship.
The system shall support terminating a peering relationship cleanly.
The system shall provide monitoring of who shared what and when.
The system should include automated capacity-triggered peer selection.
The system should be able to automatically activate peers in some cases.
The system should select the most appropriate peers based on the agreed policies.
The system should provide controls to prevent traffic from being routed somewhere it should not be routed.
Traffic redirection and selective information exchange shall be the highest-priority capabilities.
Policy negotiation and capacity-triggered peer selection shall be the next-highest-priority capabilities after traffic redirection and selective information exchange.
The remaining capabilities are important but serve as supporting functions for the core capabilities.
The system shall move user requests away from an overloaded CDN and toward a peer that has capacity.
The system shall redirect traffic in a way that causes little noticeable difference for the user.
The system shall use already agreed-upon policies to determine traffic redirection.
The system shall redirect only eligible traffic.
The system shall respect geography restrictions when redirecting traffic.
The system shall respect content rights restrictions when redirecting traffic.
The system shall respect customer-specific restrictions when redirecting traffic.
The system shall switch traffic back cleanly once the system's own capacity recovers.
If a redirect is not allowed, the system shall keep the request on its own side and apply normal fallback behavior.
If a redirect is not allowed and fallback is needed, the system may use local throttling or queueing.
If no suitable peer is available, the system shall leave the request unredirected.
If no suitable peer is available, the system shall alert operations.
When a redirect does not happen, the reason shall be visible so that the team can act on it quickly.
The system shall allow sharing only the operational data needed for peering to work.
The system shall not expose internal customer data or other sensitive business details.
The system shall allow different peers to share different levels of detail.
The system shall let users define what is visible to whom.
The system shall support accounting records between peers so that usage can be reconciled later without disclosing more than necessary.
The system shall allow sharing measurements needed for billing or settlement tied to the peering relationship and not individual end users.
The system shall allow sharing summary performance indicators such as latency or error rates when they help a peer make routing decisions.
The system shall never share customer identity.
The system shall never share individual request logs.
The system shall never share contract details with the system's own customers.
The system shall never share content metadata that would reveal private business information unless explicitly allowed.
The system shall support peer discovery through a controlled registry.
The system shall support peer discovery through direct invitations.
The system shall support both peer discovery paths: controlled registry and direct invitations.
The system shall require approval steps before anything becomes active.
Policy negotiation should use a combination of automated handling and manual approval.
The system should use predefined templates to handle common cases automatically.
The system should require manual approval for unusual or higher-risk policy negotiations.
New regions should be treated as unusual or higher-risk cases that require manual approval.
Special content classes should be treated as unusual or higher-risk cases that require manual approval.
Large capacity commitments should be treated as unusual or higher-risk cases that require manual approval.
The system should clearly surface proposed terms so an operator can confirm or adjust them before the agreement goes live.
The operations team shall be involved in the project because it will monitor capacity, handle failures, and deal with incidents.
Legal and compliance stakeholders shall be involved because sharing rules, privacy boundaries, and settlement terms must stay within policy and contract limits.
Partner CDN engineering teams shall provide input to define which information and control signals are practical to exchange and to avoid making the integration too brittle.
The system shall absorb traffic spikes by using peers without disrupting users.
The system shall absorb traffic spikes by using peers without exposing sensitive data.
The system shall be reliable enough to allow peering relationships to be turned on without manual chaos.
The system shall be reliable enough to allow peering relationships to be adjusted without manual chaos.
The system shall be reliable enough to allow peering relationships to be ended without manual chaos.
The system shall ensure that accounting reconciles cleanly after peering relationships are turned on, adjusted, or ended.
The system shall provide operational visibility into what is happening.
The system shall make policy decisions trustworthy to operations users.
The system shall support resilience during partial failures.
If a peer becomes unavailable or control-plane communication is lost, the system shall fail back gracefully rather than blackholing traffic or making bad routing decisions.
The system shall provide a clear audit trail for policy changes and traffic actions so that incidents or disputes can be explained afterward.
The system shall enable separate CDN operators to work together when one of them becomes overloaded.
The system shall reduce the need for each CDN operator to overbuild for every traffic spike independently.
The system shall help CDN operators find trusted peers.
The system shall help CDN operators set up the terms for sharing capacity and content.
The system shall route traffic so end users continue to receive good service when demand shifts quickly.
Traffic patterns are becoming more volatile, especially for live events, launches, and regional surges.
It is expensive to keep enough spare capacity everywhere all the time.
Customers expect low latency and high availability.
If a provider cannot absorb a spike locally, it risks service degradation or losing business.
Peering should let providers share burden more flexibly.
The business side must be able to control trust, pricing, and who gets access to what.
Network operations and traffic engineering shall be the main day-to-day users within a CDN provider.
Network operations and traffic engineering shall watch demand.
Network operations and traffic engineering shall approve peer relationships.
Network operations and traffic engineering shall manage routing behavior.
Business development or partnership teams shall handle commercial agreements and policy terms.
Accounting or finance shall care about settlement and usage reports.
Peer CDN operators shall use the same infrastructure on their side.
Customers with strict requirements may influence what content can or cannot be shared.
Customers with strict requirements probably shall not log into the system directly.
Network operations require fast and reliable visibility into available peer capacity.
Network operations require visibility into current load.
Network operations require safe ways to redirect traffic without causing a bad user experience.
Business development requires clear policy controls.
Business development requires proof that a peer is trustworthy.
Business development requires the ability to negotiate terms such as scope, duration, and what content or regions are included.
Accounting requires accurate usage records and agreed measurement rules.
Accounting requires the ability to reconcile who provided what capacity and settle it without disputes.
Discovery shall expose only a controlled profile initially.
The controlled profile shall include capacity ranges.
The controlled profile shall include regions served.
The controlled profile shall include high-level policy attributes.
Discovery shall not expose full internal network details at the initial stage.
Negotiation shall happen in stages.
Each side shall reveal more information only after authentication and a trust check.
Each provider shall be able to mark certain data as private or shareable only with specific peers.
The system shall consistently enforce data-sharing rules so that a peer cannot see or use information outside the agreed scope.
The system should not hard-code too much jargon because shared terminology varies by team and company.
The system should present capacity-related concepts in a consistent way.
The system should support standard terms.
The system should allow provider-specific labels where needed.
External CDN operators shall interact with the system through authenticated partner interfaces rather than open public access.
The authenticated partner interfaces shall support both automated system-to-system exchange and a human-facing portal for exceptions or review.
Peer access shall be tightly scoped so that a peer can see only the regions, content categories, or capacity data that it has been granted.
Sensitive internal telemetry shall remain hidden from peers.
Customers shall have limited direct interaction with the peering system.
Customer input shall come mainly as policy signals or contractual constraints through administrative workflows rather than direct operational access to the peering system.
The system shall maintain one canonical underlying meaning behind the scenes.
The system shall allow each provider to map its own labels to the shared canonical model.
The system shall display the term each audience is used to seeing.
The system shall provide tooltips or definitions in the user interface so users can confirm they are referring to the same thing before approving policies or agreements.
The system shall version terminology mappings.
If two providers use the same term differently, the system shall flag the situation as an ambiguity.
Capacity data and policy data shall be created or updated by the owning provider whenever its operational state changes.
Usage records and accounting records shall be retained for a longer period than other data types.
The exact retention period for usage records and accounting records is undefined and must be confirmed with finance and legal.
Some records shall be immutable for audit purposes.
The platform should mostly automate lifecycle handling.
The platform should send alerts before anything is archived or deleted.
The platform should keep an audit trail showing what happened, when, and under whose policy.
The platform should require a final approval step before permanent deletion of sensitive or legally important data.
The system shall provide a structured way for users to resolve terminology conflicts instead of only displaying an error.
The platform shall provide lightweight learning support built into the platform.
Accessibility is important for the platform.
For peer discovery and negotiation, the system shall respond fast enough to be usable interactively by operators.
For traffic redirection, the system shall propagate decisions quickly enough to react to traffic spikes without causing visible service degradation.
The system shall remain predictable under load and degrade gracefully instead of making bad routing decisions.
Capacity shall mean the amount of traffic a peer can safely absorb at the network edge and for any shared origin or cache resources involved.
The system shall allow some capacity information to be shared directly between peers.
The system shall allow each provider to hide sensitive details such as exact utilization, topology, and customer-specific constraints.
The system shall allow each provider to expose only the level of precision it is comfortable with.
The system shall quickly detect when a peer or region becomes unhealthy.
The platform shall prioritize alerts so that only urgent issues wake people up during peak load.
The system should support running old and new components in parallel for a period during migration.
The system should preserve active agreements during migration.
The system should preserve routing state during migration.
The system should preserve accounting data during migration.
Customer-facing or traffic-affecting changes should use maintenance windows or automatic draining to avoid abrupt cutover.
The system shall preserve the original provider-specific values.
The system shall preserve conversion rules.
The system shall maintain an audit trail of original provider-specific values and conversion rules.
Only truly service-impacting issues should trigger immediate alerts.
Failed redirection should be treated as an immediate alert condition.
Widespread peer unavailability should be treated as an immediate alert condition.
Negotiation outages that prevent traffic spillover should be treated as an immediate alert condition.
Accounting corruption that could affect settlements should be treated as an immediate alert condition.
A single peer health degradation should go to a normal operational queue instead of paging someone immediately.
A noncritical configuration mismatch should go to a normal operational queue instead of paging someone immediately.
The system shall validate data types.
The system shall validate ranges.
The system shall validate required fields.
The system shall provide a trace from each canonical value back to the source value and mapping rule.
The system shall suppress duplicate alerts.
The system shall continue updating the same incident instead of creating new incidents for the same root cause.
The system shall escalate an incident only if the problem crosses a severity threshold, spreads, or lasts long enough to require human intervention.
Capacity problems occur during sudden traffic spikes.
Capacity problems occur when edge capacity in a region becomes too limited.
Capacity problems occur during localized outages.
Capacity problems occur when demand shifts faster than the team can provision additional resources.
Other CDNs should absorb overflow traffic so users continue receiving low-latency service instead of failures or severe slowdowns.
The system should support content replication and request redirection to move load quickly and keep service levels stable while protecting information that each provider does not want to expose.
The system shall start offloading before hard saturation is reached.
The system shall base offloading decisions on CPU utilization, bandwidth, cache pressure, and request latency.
The system shall not use one universal offloading threshold.
The system shall vary offloading policy by site and by content type.
The system shall consider the rate at which demand is rising when deciding whether to offload.
The system shall trigger collaboration early enough that users do not notice degradation.
The system shall receive requests at the edge.
The system shall determine where a request should be served from.
If the requested content is already cached locally, the system shall return it immediately.
If the requested content is not cached locally, the system shall fetch it from the origin or a nearby upstream cache.
After fetching uncached content, the system shall deliver it back to the user.
After delivering content, the system shall usually keep or update the cached copy depending on the content policy.
When content is marked shareable and the system is under pressure, it may route the request to a peer CDN or receive it from one.
In the normal case, the request shall stay within the system's own delivery path.
The system shall discover peer CDN candidates from a trusted registry or exchange of peers.
The system shall check whether peer CDN candidates are reachable.
The system shall check whether peer CDN candidates are currently willing to participate in the relevant region or service class.
The system shall determine whether peer CDN candidates have available capacity.
The system shall determine whether peer CDN candidates support the required geography.
The system shall determine whether peer CDN candidates can handle the content type or traffic profile being handled.
The system shall collect current load information from peer CDN candidates.
The system shall collect capacity headroom information from peer CDN candidates.
The system shall collect supported protocol information from peer CDN candidates.
The system shall collect policy constraint information from peer CDN candidates.
The system shall collect information about any limits on what data peer CDN candidates are willing to share.
The system shall provide enough information to decide quickly whether a peer CDN candidate is a safe and useful match.
Peer capabilities shall be treated as dynamic rather than as a one-time promise.
If a peer’s available headroom drops or its policy changes, the peer shall update the system quickly.
When a peer’s available headroom drops or its policy changes, the system shall recalculate whether the peer is still suitable before sending more traffic.
If a change happens after offload has already started, the system shall taper traffic down or shift it elsewhere without interrupting users.
The system shall avoid relying on stale information.
The system shall exchange the minimum information needed to measure how much capacity was consumed and how it changed over time.
The system shall exchange request counts.
The system shall exchange bytes served.
The system shall exchange an approximate service class.
The system shall exchange the time window covered by the traffic.
The system shall provide a view of current headroom and any per-peer limits so that peers are not overcommitted.
Both sides shall agree on the same measurement basis for accounting.
The system shall support later reconciliation if traffic shifts mid-stream or is retried.
The system should use different timing targets for different traffic classes.
The system shall not consume peer capacity in a way that violates the agreement or starves the peer’s own obligations.
The collaboration shall help when the local site is in trouble.
The system shall preserve control over what is owned locally versus what is borrowed.
Each participant shall own its own infrastructure.
Each participant shall own its own capacity planning.
Each participant shall enforce its local policies.
The peer shall accept traffic only when it has agreed capacity.
The peer shall serve authorized content.
The peer shall report usage accurately for accounting and settlement.
Our side shall own the steering decision.
Our side shall own the rules for when to reduce the relationship.
Before sharing traffic, onboarding shall cover trust.
Before sharing traffic, onboarding shall cover policy alignment.
The parties shall agree on what information can be exchanged.
The parties shall agree on the escalation path and rollback path if something goes wrong.
The new provider shall be introduced without disrupting existing service.
The system shall exchange enough configuration data to recognize each party during onboarding.
The system shall exchange enough configuration data to route traffic correctly during onboarding.
The system shall exchange enough configuration data to enforce agreed policies without exposing unnecessary internal detail.
The system shall include capacity limits in the configuration data exchanged during onboarding.
The negotiation shall confirm that both sides agree on the scope of the relationship.
The rollout shall be paused whenever confidence in the data or the control path is lost, even if there has been no hard failure yet.
The system shall prioritize capabilities that reduce risk and make the collaboration safe before capabilities that increase scale.
The system shall limit replication to content that is allowed by rights and by the peer agreement.
For most replicated content, peer copies should track the origin closely enough that users do not see obviously outdated material.
Each side shall provide enough load information to support routing and capacity decisions.
The system shall not require every internal metric to be shared.
The collaboration governance authority should be defined now.
If the parties cannot agree on who can change what, the governance authority should be recorded as undecided and the relationship should remain limited until governance is settled.
If a field cannot be shared, the system should use a substitute that preserves the operational meaning.
The system may tolerate omissions without a substitute when the omitted information is truly nonessential and does not affect billing or routing.
The system must explicitly flag omissions that impact settlement, capacity trust, or policy enforcement.
If something important is omitted, the other side must be informed that the exchange is incomplete so they do not make decisions based on assumed full visibility.
The system should be mostly automated and event-driven.
The system shall log what changed.
The system shall log who or what authorized the resumption.
The system shall gradually re-enable traffic rather than turning everything back on at once.
If anything is ambiguous, the system shall require a human approval step before full resumption.
For interactive or highly time-sensitive traffic, the steering decision shall occur very quickly, in the low tens of milliseconds, to remain useful during an overflow.

For less sensitive traffic classes such as large downloads or background delivery, the system may tolerate more delay, but the steering decision shall still be fast enough to avoid repeated user failures.
A cross-CDN redirect is too slow if it adds more pain than the overload it is intended to avoid, including cases where retries, timeouts, or visible stalls are already occurring.
The acceptable steering delay shall depend on the traffic class, and the system should act before the client experience degrades noticeably.
The system should usually provide a grace period when ending a collaboration so traffic can be drained or rehomed in an orderly way instead of cutting the peer off immediately.
The grace period may be extended if there are active long-running transfers or a scheduled termination that both sides agreed to.
In an emergency, such as a security incident, the system should bypass the grace period and stop routing right away.
The grace period shall not exceed the limit allowed by business or security policy.
The grace period should be based on the longest acceptable session or transfer type for the collaboration.
The grace period may be extended only if both sides agree and there are legitimate in-flight workloads that would be disrupted by cutting over too quickly.
The system shall end the grace period early when continued service becomes unsafe or noncompliant.
For in-flight sessions or transfers, the shutdown shall attempt clean failover to a safe alternate peer when one is available.
For in-flight sessions or transfers, if no safe alternate peer is available, the shutdown shall terminate them in a controlled way and record what was interrupted.
The exact duration rule for the grace period is undecided for the moment.
The exact duration rule depends on the traffic mix and the contracts the system ends up supporting.
The shutdown shall stop accepting new traffic before terminating the session or transfer.
The shutdown shall send an appropriate notification to affected systems and operators.
If there is customer-facing impact, the event shall be flagged for later reporting or reconciliation.
The system shall require a basic readiness check on both sides before traffic is shared.
The system shall require a test or limited pilot route before broad traffic goes live.
The system shall use the pilot route to confirm content replication before broad traffic goes live.
The system shall ensure that the new provider can absorb the intended traffic class without causing latency spikes.
The system shall ensure that the new provider can absorb the intended traffic class without causing cache misses.
The system shall ensure that the new provider can absorb the intended traffic class without causing policy violations on either side.
The system shall classify a termination as graceful when the collaboration is ended by a normal business decision and traffic is drained within the planned window, even if the full timeout is used.
The system shall classify a termination as forced for reporting and customer-impact purposes when it must be cut short because of an incident, breach, or failed failover.
The system shall treat a termination as forced for reporting and customer-impact purposes even if some cleanup steps were still attempted.
The system shall provide a peer-to-peer control interface for operational coordination.
The peer-to-peer control interface shall handle capacity updates.
The peer-to-peer control interface shall be authenticated and encrypted.
Collaboration policies shall be versioned and negotiated rather than edited in place.
When demand or business conditions change, either side shall be able to propose a policy revision.
A peer shall be allowed to reject incoming traffic if it is over capacity.
A peer shall not stop serving content that was already authorized unless there is an emergency.
Delaying usage reporting shall only be allowed for a short operational window.
The agreement shall explicitly define the operational limits.
A peer shall not quietly withhold service beyond what was approved.
Older peers shall be expected to keep operating safely within a defined compatibility window.
The system shall permit an incompatible protocol change only if it solves a material business or security problem that cannot be addressed with a compatible upgrade.
The system shall limit the scope of the affected peering relationship so that not every partnership is at risk at once.
An environment shall be rejected if the required records for settlement and dispute handling cannot be obtained.
A peer location is unacceptable if local law forces disclosure of traffic records in a way that conflicts with agreed privacy commitments.
Hosting terms are unacceptable if they let the provider retain logs beyond the customer's control.
Hosting terms are unacceptable if they block the customer from deleting records when the relationship ends.
Data residency or surveillance rules are disqualifying if they make it impossible to meet retention obligations consistently.
Discovery and advertising shall be policy-driven.
A peer shall publish only the capabilities it has explicitly approved for external use.
A peer shall not expose internal topology unless it has been separately authorized.
Advertised information shall be scoped by region.
The discovery view shall update quickly enough after a permission change so that the system does not keep offering information it is no longer allowed to share.

If the same service degradation repeats across multiple peak periods, the system or operations process shall treat this as a sign that the fix is not stable and shall move to rollback as soon as the pattern is confirmed.
The system or operations process may stay in limited service only when the impact is clearly contained, the cause is understood, and the situation shows improvement rather than repetition.
If users are still being materially affected or the failure mode cannot be isolated, the system or operations process shall prioritize rollback.
A peer is primarily responsible for enforcing its local policies.
A provider's responsibility becomes shared or escalated when the peer's enforcement failure affects traffic sent or received under the peering arrangement.
When a peer's enforcement failure affects traffic under the peering arrangement, the other provider should intervene first by throttling the affected exchange.
If usage reporting is inaccurate, the provider that owns the disputed records should investigate and correct them.
If the problem is severe enough that the relationship can no longer be trusted, either side should be able to escalate to formal suspension or termination.
The system shall require a clear operational trigger before either side can move to suspension or termination.
When it is safe to do so, the system shall provide notice and an opportunity to correct the issue before escalation.
Before escalation, the invoking side shall document the reason for escalation.
Before escalation, the system shall ensure traffic is safely rerouted or drained to avoid creating a wider outage.
Notice and a chance to cure should be required when the issue is operational or commercial and there is no immediate threat to users, data, or the network.
A cure period should be expected before suspension or termination for a normal policy breach, a billing disagreement, or a capacity shortfall that can be corrected safely.
Immediate action is justified when there is active abuse, a security compromise, unlawful traffic handling, or a condition that could quickly cascade into broader service impact.
In urgent cases, either party should be able to cut off or limit the exchange right away and notify the other party as soon as practical.
Obviously falsified usage data justifies immediate action for a load or accounting problem.
Traffic levels that are putting the peering relationship at risk right now justify immediate action for a load or accounting problem.
The deciding boundary is whether the peer can still be trusted to exchange traffic safely while it corrects the problem.
If trust is lost because the evidence shows deliberate manipulation or an ongoing inability to measure accurately, the response should be suspension before resolving the details.

The system should be considered safe to expand only when the limited rollout has been stable for a meaningful period and is providing the expected relief on the overloaded side without creating new hotspots elsewhere.
Before full trust and stability are established, the peer control interface shall carry only the minimum information needed to keep the peering relationship safe and functional.
Administrators shall be able to understand the basic workflow quickly enough to approve peers, review status, and handle simple operational actions without a lot of training.
Older peers shall be allowed to remain on the previous protocol version only for a defined transition period.
A peer may remain temporarily on the previous version if it still meets minimum security and interoperability requirements.
The discovery view shall refresh essentially immediately after a permission change is committed.
The system shall hold back from offloading traffic to a peer if the peer is showing instability, even when the latency prediction looks good.
Some content classes should have explicit freshness rules.
The system should stop replication or serving when content can no longer be validated within its required freshness window.
Serving stale data is worse than serving nothing.
Long-lived static assets may use a much looser threshold.
If a content class has no agreed validation interval, it should be treated conservatively.
Visibility of shared capabilities shall vary by partner relationship type.
The scope of visibility shall be based on the negotiated agreement and the minimum necessary exposure principle.
The system shall share only the minimum necessary request information to complete the handoff.
The system shall share content only if the peer is authorized to store or serve it under the replication policy.
The system shall reject or redirect a request or object if its privacy restrictions cannot be preserved across the handoff, keeping that information local.
The system shall define the main collaboration triggers now.
Overflow handoff shall occur only when local capacity is nearing a configured threshold.
Peers behind shared infrastructure or in a multi-tenant environment shall be treated as having weaker isolation unless there is explicit evidence of separation and control.
If the operator cannot guarantee administrative control or log integrity in a region, the peer shall be excluded from higher-trust relationships or limited to a very narrow, low-sensitivity role.
Location alone shall not disqualify a peer from trust relationships.
The system shall delay or block an overflow handoff whenever the peer is no longer authorized for the traffic class.
The system shall keep traffic local or fail over to another approved peer if eligibility cannot be verified quickly enough.
